The striated darter (Etheostoma striatulum) is a small, benthic freshwater fish endemic to the upper Duck River system in Tennessee. Field surveys indicate that individuals rarely exceed a body length of 5.6 cm [Li = 5.6 cm], making it one of the smaller members of the speciose genus Etheostoma. This modest ultimate total length is consistent with the species' occupation of restricted, headwater stream habitats where selective pressures may favour a diminutive adult size. Young-of-the-year individuals captured during late summer collections typically measure between 2.0 and 2.5 cm, suggesting that the first growing season is a period of rapid somatic expansion before energy is diverted toward reproductive development.

The onset of gonadal maturation in this species occurs at a notably small body size compared to many sympatric congeners. Histological examination of field-collected specimens reveals that sexual maturity is attained at a total length of approximately 2.7 cm [Lp = approximately 2.7 cm], a threshold based on length-frequency data from the species' natal streams. Individuals reaching this size are capable of gamete production, though their reproductive contribution may be limited by the physical constraints of the small body cavity. The precocious maturation schedule likely reflects an adaptive response to high adult mortality rates, favouring early breeding despite reduced per-capita fecundity at first reproduction.

Reproduction in Etheostoma striatulum begins with the deposition of demersal, adhesive eggs within interstitial gravel spaces of shallow riffles. Based on field measurements of ovum diameter, each newly fertilised egg measures approximately 2.0 mm across, yielding a calculated wet weight at birth of roughly 0.0042 g [Wwb = roughly 0.0042 g]. This minute initial mass is characteristic of darter species that produce large numbers of small, yolk-laden eggs, maximising the probability of larval survival in the unpredictable flow regimes typical of headwater environments. The alevin stage is brief, with yolk-sac resorption completed within a few days of eclosion, after which the free-swimming larvae must locate suitable feeding habitat.

Adult body condition in this species is constrained by the same allometric scaling relationships observed across the genus. The estimated ultimate wet weight for a fully grown individual at the asymptotic length of 5.6 cm is 1.15 g [Wwi = 1.15 g], derived from a length-weight conversion applied to field-caught specimens. This value places the striated darter among the lightest-bodied members of its clade, consistent with its elongated, streamlined morphology and preference for swift-flowing microhabitats. The modest adult mass may also reflect the energetic costs of maintaining position in high-velocity currents, which imposes a premium on a slender, low-drag body plan.

The maximum lifespan documented for this species under natural stream conditions, derived from mark-recapture studies conducted over multiple years, is 730 days [am = 730 days] at mean annual water temperatures of approximately 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This relatively short life span aligns with the species' early-maturing, high-investment reproductive strategy, where individuals channel available resources into one or two spawning seasons before succumbing to senescence or environmentally mediated mortality. The thermal regime of the natal streams plays a critical role in governing metabolic rates and, consequently, the pace of life-history progression. Comparative data from congeneric species inhabiting warmer tailwaters suggest that longevity may be reduced under elevated temperatures, underscoring the sensitivity of this species to thermal habitat degradation.
